site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Lakshmana Receives His Gifts
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 11 (Gita Press translation)
body: In the Dandaka forest, where rakshasas threatened the sages, the great rishi Agastya came to meet Rama and brought him divine gifts: the bow of Vishnu, quivers of inexhaustible arrows, and the shining blade of Parashurama's line. With folded hands, Lakshmana stood ready at his elder brother's side.

Agastya then turned gently to Lakshmana and shared a deeper teaching. The strongest weapon any warrior could wield, he said, was unwavering attention and devotion to the one he served. Steady presence, not force, was the true armor.

Lakshmana received these words with folded hands and a humble heart. From that day forward, his watchfulness over Rama only deepened, and a quiet strength settled between the brothers as they walked together through the sacred woods.

stories.title: The Snake Who Became a Friend
stories.source: The Jataka, Vol. II (E. B. Cowell ed., 1895), No. 173 · Nakulapita Jataka
body: Deep in the storied tales of the Jataka, a snake tired of his born enmity toward the mice. He left off hunting them and slipped quietly into the household of one mouse family, becoming a trusted and gentle companion who shared their nest without harm.

One terrible day a mongoose, the snake's own natural foe, came snarling at the door. The eldest mouse leapt to defend his family and was wounded in the fight. Bleeding and faint, he called softly for his reptile friend, and the snake came swiftly to his side.

Guarding the little house until the mouse could heal, the snake kept watch as the mongoose never returned. In that quiet, steady vigil the old hatreds melted away, and the bond between snake and mice became a living proof that even the deepest enmities can be set aside.

stories.title: The Faithful Guardian Mongoose
stories.source: The Jataka, Vol. III (E. B. Cowell ed., 1897), No. 373 · Mongoose Jataka
body: During a long famine in the Indian countryside, a kind family and their pet mongoose shared what little they had. When a visiting monk arrived at their humble dwelling, the householders offered their very last piece of meat, a precious gift made from their final stores, and stepped out on an errand, trusting the mongoose to guard the home.

The little guardian circled the house with quiet devotion, watching over the threshold. Upon returning, the family found the monk seated peacefully, and he asked the mongoose to bless his newborn child, who lay sleeping nearby.

The mongoose padded softly to the infant, curled tenderly around the tiny body in a protective embrace, and looked up with a warm, contented smile. The monk, moved by this gentle creature's faithful heart, praised the selfless love guarding his blessed child.

stories.title: King Shibi's Unflinching Gift
body: In the kingdom of the famed King Shibi, a dove fluttered into his lap seeking refuge, chased close behind by a hawk who named the bird his lawful prey. Shibi offered the hawk other flesh in trade, but the hawk would only accept flesh weighed fairly against the dove.

Shibi bared his own body and laid himself upon the scale, strip by strip, steady and unflinching beside the trembling dove. When at last he offered his whole self, the hawk and dove stood revealed as gods, their disguises falling away in light.

The gods blessed Shibi for the perfection of his giving. His wounds closed whole, his kingdom flourished, and across every age his name is praised as a bright example of compassion that does not hold back.

stories.title: Sixteen Forever, in Markandeya's Arms
body: A child sage named Markandeya learned that fate had granted him only sixteen years upon the earth. Instead of fear, he answered with devotion, spending every day from his earliest years worshipping Lord Shiva, chanting the great lord's holy names and pressing his heart against the sacred lingam.

When the appointed hour arrived and Yama's messengers came to carry his soul away, the boy did not let go. He clung tightly to the lingam and sang praise with all his breath. From the stone itself, Shiva rose in terrible beauty, roaring at the messengers and driving them from his beloved child.

The lord decreed that Markandeya would be sixteen years old forever, untouched by age or death. So the young sage rose from the floor a radiant youth, blessed for his single-hearted love, a quiet reminder that unshakable devotion can turn even the final hour into a gift.
